narrative:
The model predicted a 72.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you. By far the strongest factor was your LSAT score of 23. This score is substantially below the average of students who were accepted, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year law school grades, which placed you in the third decile, also worked against you, though with less force; they were noticeably lower than the average sixth-decile performance of accepted students and added further weight toward a negative outcome. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20, while slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, actually pulled the prediction slightly in the opposite direction, offering a small counterbalance toward success.

Taken together, the low LSAT score and weaker early law school performance created a picture of elevated risk that outweighed the modest positive signal from your college grades.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, while also working to improve your academic performance in the coming year. These steps will directly address the factors that led to the rejection and improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
